rows.speaker: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and other Companions
rows.claim: Companions identified “the friend by your side” as one's wife or husband.
rows.anchor: According to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and other Companions, "the friend by your side" (as-sahib bi'l-janb) is one's wife or husband (Tabari).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, those whom one's right hand possesses are enslaved people of either sex.
rows.anchor: By "those whom you rightfully possess" (lit., "whom your right hands possess") are meant, in this context, slaves of either sex.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because freeing a slave is the best good one can do for them, the command elliptically calls for emancipation; 2:177 and 9:60 explicitly make freeing people a zakah objective.
rows.anchor: Since this verse enjoins the "doing of good" towards all people with whom one is in contact, and since the best that can be done to a slave is to free him, the above passage calls, elliptically, for the freeing of slaves (Manar V, 94).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that the earth would become level with them.
rows.anchor: Lit., "become level with them".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The apostle” is probably generic, referring to every apostle who preached God's message across time.
rows.anchor: The term "the apostle" is probably used here in its generic sense, and refers to all the apostles who preached God's message at one time or another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer instruction follows the Judgment Day discussion: prayer is an earthly spiritual encounter with God that reminds people of their responsibility to the Creator.
rows.anchor: The reference to prayer at this place arises from the mention, in the preceding verses, of the Day of Judgment, when man will have to answer before God for what he did during his life in this world

rows.speaker: some of the commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators regard the ban on praying drunk as an initial stage of total intoxicant prohibition, later abrogated by 5:90.
rows.anchor: some of the commentators assume that this ordinance represented the first stage of the total prohibition of intoxicants, and has been, consequently, "abrogated" by the promulgation of the law of total abstinence from all intoxicants (5:90).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects abrogation as untenable and says nothing warrants treating this continuing safeguard as redundant after the general intoxicant ban; he also rejects the abrogation doctrine in 2:106.
rows.anchor: the doctrine of "abrogation" is entirely untenable (see surah 2, verse 106), there is no warrant whatever for regarding the above verse as a "first step" which has become redundant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people remain vulnerable to lapses, this verse prevents adding sinful prayer while drunk to the separate sin of using intoxicants.
rows.anchor: since "man has been created weak" (4:28), his lapse from the way of virtue is always a possibility: and it is to prevent him from adding the sin of praying while in a state of drunkenness to the sin of using intoxicants as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukr covers any mental disequilibrium, including drugs, giddiness, passion, or metaphorical drunkenness from sleep, not only alcohol.
rows.anchor: the expression "while you are in a state of drunkenness (sukara)" does not apply exclusively to alcoholic intoxication, since the term sukr, in its wider connotation, signifies any state of mental disequilibrium

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since worship requires consciousness, prayer is allowed only when a person has full mental faculties and knows what they are saying.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an insists throughout on consciousness as an indispensable element in every act of worship, prayer is permitted only when man is in full possession of his mental faculties and "knows what he is saying".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Junub describes the state after sexual intercourse; from janaba, “to make remote,” it denotes distance from prayer due to immersion in sexual passion.
rows.anchor: The term junub (rendered by me as "in a state requiring total ablution") is derived from the verb janaba, "he made (a thing) remote", and signifies one's remoteness from prayer because of immersion in sexual passion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally refers to coming from the place where one relieves oneself.
rows.anchor: Lit., "if one of you comes from the place in which one satisfies...", etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tayammum is performed by touching earth or a dust-bearing substance with the palms, then lightly wiping the face and hands.
rows.anchor: This symbolic ablution, called tayammum, consists in touching the earth, or anything supposed to contain dust, with the palms of one's hands and then passing them lightly over face and hands.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When water is unavailable or cannot be used due to illness, tayammum replaces both the full bath after intercourse and the partial pre-prayer ablution.
rows.anchor: Whenever water is not within reach - or cannot be used because of illness - the tayammum takes the place of both the total ablution after sexual intercourse (ghusl) and the partial ablution before prayers (wudu).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who deem themselves pure are Jews claiming chosen status and Christians who rely on Jesus' vicarious atonement for humanity's sins.
rows.anchor: the Jews, who consider, themselves to be "God's chosen people" and, therefore, a priori destined for God's grace, and the Christians, who believe in Jesus' "vicarious atonement" for the sins of mankind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Christians profess one God, elevating Jesus to divine manifestation and worshipping saints assigns divine or semi-divine status to humans and constitutes deeper shirk.
rows.anchor: the Christians by their elevation of Jesus to the status of a manifestation of God in human form and their open worship of a hierarchy of saints

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews' attribution of overriding lawmaking authority to Talmudic scholars is also shirk; Asad compares this to 9:31.
rows.anchor: the Jews by their attribution of law-giving powers to the great Talmudic scholars, whose legal verdicts are supposed to override, if need be, any ordinance of the scriptures (cf. in this respect 9: 31).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condemnation also applies to Muslims who worship saints or give them reverence due to God alone.
rows.anchor: It goes without saying that this condemnation applies also to those Muslims who have fallen into the sin of worshipping saints and according them something of the reverence which is due to God alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, the phrase covers people who claim belief in one God yet commit shirk in its deeper sense; this connects the warning to the preceding verse's shirk.
rows.anchor: the expression "those who consider themselves pure" comprises, in this context, all who think of themselves as believing in the One God (simply because they do not consciously worship a plurality of deities) but are, nevertheless, guilty of the sin of shirk in the deeper sense of this term.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatil is a slender thread rolled between the fingers, also used for the tiny fiber in a date stone's cleft; idiomatically it means a hair's breadth.
rows.anchor: a 'fatil' is any "slender thread which one rolls between one's fingers" - a term which is also, but by no means exclusively, applied to the tiny fibre adhering to the cleft of the date-stone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purity is not a group's privilege and is possible only through God's grace, since humanity is weak; Asad also points to 53:32.
rows.anchor: the above passage implies, firstly, that spiritual purity is not the privilege of any particular group or community, and, secondly, that one can become or remain pure only by God's grace, for "man has been created weak" (verse 28 above). See also note on the second paragraph of 53:32.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the replacement of burnt skins as an allegory emphasizing the long duration of afterlife suffering.
rows.anchor: This awesome allegory of suffering in the life to come is obviously meant to bring out the long-lasting nature of that suffering (Razi).

rows.speaker: all lexicographers
rows.claim: Khamr derives from khamara, “to conceal or obscure,” and denotes any substance that obscures the intellect and intoxicates.
rows.anchor: According to all the lexicographers, the word khamr (derived from the verb khamara, "he concealed" or "obscured") denotes every substance the use of which obscures the intellect, i.e., intoxicates.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition covers drugs with intoxicating effects as well as alcoholic drinks.
rows.anchor: Hence, the prohibition of intoxicants laid down in this verse comprises not merely alcoholic drinks, but also drugs which have a similar effect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sole exception is strict dire necessity, such as illness or bodily accident making intoxicants imperative and unavoidable, under 5:3.
rows.anchor: The only exception from this total prohibition arises in cases of "dire necessity" (in the strictest sense of these words), as stipulated in the last sentence of verse 3 of this surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes ansab metaphorically for idolatrous practices broadly, including saint worship, attributing magic to objects, and superstitious taboos.
rows.anchor: This term has, I believe, been used here metaphorically, and is meant to circumscribe all practices of an idolatrous nature - like saint-worship, the attribution of "magic" properties to certain inanimate objects, the observance of all manner of superstitious taboos

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For his explanation of al-azlam (“divining-arrows”), Asad directs readers to his note on 5:3.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of the expression rendered by me as "divining of the future" (al-azlam, lit., "divining-arrows"), see note 9 on the second paragraph of verse 3 of this surah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction is to leave until they immerse themselves in conversation on another subject.
rows.anchor: Lit., "until they immerse themselves in talk other than this".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links this verse to his note 90 on 5:90.
rows.anchor: See surah 5, note 90.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun and moon follow a definite reckoning.
rows.anchor: Lit., "to be [according to] a definite reckoning".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the following sequence uses present tense, the sentence is in past tense, obliquely pointing to life's original creation from water, as in 21:30.
rows.anchor: In contrast with its sequence, which is governed by the present tense, the whole of the above sentence is expressed in the past tense - thus indicating, obliquely, the original, basic aspect of God's creating life "out of water"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plants share basic principles of life and growth but differ in physiology, appearance, and taste.
rows.anchor: all so alike in the basic principles of their life and growth, and yet so different in physiology, appearance and taste.

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: Commentators agree that the one who was dead is metaphorical: a person made spiritually alive through faith who can then navigate life without error.
rows.anchor: All the commentators agree in that the expression "he who was dead" is metaphorical, and that it refers to people who become spiritually alive through faith

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the jinn here as evil shayatin and assume those beings are being addressed.
rows.anchor: According to most of the commentators, the invisible beings (al-jinn) referred to here are the "evil forces" (shayatin) among them, such as are spoken of in verse 112 of this surah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although ma'shar commonly denotes a community or genus of sentient beings sharing characteristics, that usage is based on the verb for intimate consorting.
rows.anchor: this term is often used to denote a group or community or genus of sentient beings which have certain characteristics in common: a conventional - and undoubtedly justifiable - use

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From its primary sense and verbal origin, ma'shar means close associates or family, those who live in intimate communion.
rows.anchor: in its primary significance, a person's ma'shar denotes those who are on intimate terms or in close communion with him (cf. Lisan al-'Arab: "A man's ma'shar is his family")

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the address as misguided humans living close to evil invisible beings, seduced by verse 6:112's glittering half-truths; 6:130 supports this because apostles are human, never jinn.
rows.anchor: to my mind, the allocution yd ma'shar al-jinn does not denote, "O you community of [evil] invisible beings" but, rather, "O you who are [or "have lived"] in close communion with [evil] invisible beings": in other words, it is addressed to the misguided human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wali, plural awliya', primarily means one who is close to another; the human allies were close to the evil unseen beings.
rows.anchor: It is to be remembered that the primary meaning of wali (of which awliya' is the plural) is "one who is close [to another]".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means that God may spare them through His mercy; Asad points to 6:12.
rows.anchor: I.e., unless He graces them with His mercy (see verse 12 of this surah, and the corresponding note).

rows.speaker: some of the great Muslim theologians
rows.claim: Some theologians infer that sinners' afterlife punishment is limited by God's mercy, unlike paradise's unending bliss, citing 11:107 and prophetic reports; Asad refers to a hadith at 40:12.
rows.anchor: Some of the great Muslim theologians conclude from the above and from the similar phrase occurring in 11:107 (as well as from several well-authenticated sayings of the Prophet)

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the construction as making this dietary prohibition specific to Jews and excluding believers of later times.
rows.anchor: The construction of the above sentence makes it clear that this prohibition was imposed specifically on the Jews, to the exclusion of believers of later times (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compares the restriction with Leviticus 7:23, which forbids all fat from ox, sheep, or goat.
rows.anchor: Cf. Leviticus vii, 23 (where, however, "all manner" of fat of ox, sheep or goat is declared forbidden).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 3:93 for a related discussion.
